**R1:** Thank you for your valuable questions, which we will answer in two aspects.

From one aspect, the method proposed by [1] is a fundamental theory in the field of certified robustness, and this method only addresses the classification problem. Then many certified robustness studies in other fields are based on this theory and have similar expressions on the robustness space as Eq.3 (e.g., certified robustness for graph classification [2], Patch attack [3], Point Clouds [4]). However, in fact the treatment of input distribution, perturbation space, output form and the meaning of the parameters in these methods is relevant and innovative，our method is also similar. 

From another aspect, our contribution and differentiate point from [1] are as follows:
* First, we present the first definition (Eq. 5) of certified robustness for graph matching by introducing the RS certification analysis to the node matching stage. The research of the certified robustness of GM is an emerging and unmatured topic, which can improve the security and usability of GM algorithms.
* Second, we propose to construct a smoothing distribution using $\Sigma$ containing node correlations (for example, in Euclidean space nodes with closer distance are more similar), and use the transformation property of the positive semi-definite real symmetric matrix in Appendix A to obtain a certified space in Eq.6 which is a more general representation (rather than a radius). 
* Third, $\underline{p_{A}}$ and $\overline{p_{B}}$ in Eq.6 represent the matching probability rather than classification probability in [1]. For comparison with baselines, we use the eigenvalue property in Lemma1 to further obtain a certified radius ( $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{lower}}$ ) and two auxiliary evaluation radii ($\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{max}}$ and $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{volume}}$).
* Fourth, to certify the robustness of graph matching, we process and modify its output $\mathbf{X}$. In the paper, we use a post-binarization step that converts the relaxed matching $\mathbf{S}$ (by an arbitrary relaxed GM solver) to the node matching function set $\mathbf{F}$. Then we can certify the robustness of $\mathbf{F}$.
* In summary, we deal with the input and output properties of the graph matching problem and propose a structural smoothing distribution to construct a certified robustness function. Our method presents the first definition and strategy of certified robustness for graph matching and outperforms baselines in experiments.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies the problem of certifying the robustness of structural graph matching, where the goal is to return a matching (or assignment) between the nodes of two input graphs G1 and G2, based on node and edge attributes. A robust graph matching mechanism is supposed to be resilient to adversarial perturbations of the input. The approach taken in this paper is to cast the graph matching problem as a collection of classification problems, where each node in G1 corresponds to a classification problem, and the nodes of G2 are the possible classes. Thus, if v_i is a node in G1 and u_j is a node in G2, then classifying v_i into the class u_j means that the matching matches v_i to u_j.

This formulation allows the paper to apply the generic randomizes smoothing (RS) technique to graph matching. RS is a general technique for turning non-robust classification mechanisms into certifiably robust ones, by adding some perturbation noise to the point that needs to classified, and classifying it to the most likely class (according to the input non-robust mechanism) of the perturbed point. Casting graph matching as a collection of classification problems as above allows applying RS, by adding noise to the nodes in G1. Furthermore, the covariance matrix of the Gaussian noise is chosen to reflect the structure of the input graphs, allowing for correlation between nodes, rather than adding independent noise, which according to the paper was the approach taken in prior work.

The input of graph matching algorithms is $(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1},\mathbf{z}^{2})$, where $\mathcal{G}\_{1}$ and $\mathcal{G}\_{2}$ are two input graphs, $\mathbf{z}^{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times 2}$ and $\mathbf{z}^{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_2\times 2}$ are annotated nodes of graphs. $\mathcal{G}\_{1}=(\{\mathbf{V}\_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times n_1}, \mathbf{E}\_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_e\times m_1}\})$, $\mathbf{V}\_{1}$ and $\mathbf{E}\_{1}$ represent the feature matrix of $n_{1}$ nodes and $m_{1}$ edges (likewise for $\mathbf{V}\_{2}$ and $\mathbf{E}\_{2}$). 

In most our discussion, we focus on the certified robustness research by perturbing the position attribute of nodes $\mathbf{z}^{1}$. In Section 4.1, $\mathbf{z}^{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times 2}$ reperensents the node coordinates which are usually annotated by human labeling or node detectors. The location of nodes suffers from the labeling randomness, so its robustness is very valuable for research.

Moreover, in Appendix B, we extend the certified robustness work from perturbating node position to node features, which is $d_v$-dimension. In section4.1, we derive Theorem1 by perturbation $\mathbf{z}^{1}$ as an example, but in fact this conclusion also applies to perturbation features, as in the Appendix B. **R2:** Thank you for your very valuable suggestion, and we will add an explanation for the composition of $\mathbf{F}$: $\mathbf{F}=\{f_{i}\vert f_{i}:\left(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1}, \mathbf{z}^{2}\right)\rightarrow r_{j}, i\in n_{1}, j \in n_{2}\}$, $f_{i}$ solves for which node in $\mathbf{z}^{2}$ matches the i-th node in $\mathbf{z}^{1}$, $r_{j}$ represents the j-th node $r_{j}$ in $\mathbf{z}^{2}$.

>***Q3: Authors don’t have a good explanation for interpreting results either.***
**R3:** Thank you for your valuable questions, and we further interpret the experimental results as follows.
* In Section 5.2, we evaluate the certified robustness on deep networks when perturbing node locations. We also evaluate the certified robustness on deep networks when perturbing features in Appendix B.
We follow the evaluation metrics of [2] to compare our method and baselines by robustness radius $R$ ($\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{lower}}$, $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{max}}$ and $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{volume}}$ in paper) and certified accuracy. When the radius on $x$-axis is the same, the higher the certified accuracy on $y$-axis, the better the certified robustness of the method. For a single sample, we output the matching result of smoothed $g$ (Eq.4) and robustness radius $R$. We aggregate the results of all samples into a plot with $R$ as the $x$-axis and accuracy as the $y$-axis as in Fig.2. 
The certified accuracy of our method is slightly lower sometimes than baselines when $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{lower}}$ is small. However, when $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{lower}}$ is large, the accuracy of baseline decreases significantly or even fails completely while our method maintains a more respectable accuracy. When evaluating using $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{max}}$ and $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{volume}}$, the advantages of our method are even more obvious. 
In conclusion, our method outperforms other methods in certified robustness, and the advantage is especially evident when the perturbation is large. 
* In Section 5.3, we evaluation the certified robustness of non-learning solvers RRWM on simulation dataset, we also follow the evaluation metrics of [2]. We compare the effectiveness of our method with the baseline by perturbing node locations and edge features respectively. Our method has similar performance of the certified accuracy corresponding to the same $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{lower}}$ with the baseline. However, our method performs better on $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{volume}}$ and $\|\|\delta\|\|\_{\text{max}}$ which indicates that the guarantee space certified by our method is wider and its overall robustness is better.
* In Section 5.4, we compare the effect of the correlations strength in $\Sigma$ on robustness in Fig. 4(a). We compare the experimental results of retaining correlations, partially retaining correlations (for example, 20% means that the correlation coefficients of the top 20% are retained), and completely removing correlations to demonstrate the effectiveness of the $\Sigma$. Then we find that $\Sigma$ can trade off robustness radius and certified accuracy as in Fig. 4(b). When the $\Sigma$ is calculated by larger original $\sigma$, the radius range is wider but some accuracy is sacrificed. This experiment reveals how to set the parameters according to the requirements for application.
* We made a synchronous modification in the Section.5.

content.comment:
>***Q1: It's not obvious that there will ever be any application of these ideas (quite possibly low significance).***
> 
**R1:** Studies on robustness of machine learning models have attracted wide attention, while the robustness of combinatorial solvers (graph matching is one the cases) is an emerging and unmatured topic whose importance has also been elaborated in the previous works [1].

* Graph matching (GM) problem is an intensively studied combinatorial optimization problem in computer vision and pattern recognition (see the surveys [6,7,8]). CVPR'22 paper [1] raised people's attention that neural GM solvers can be sensitive to (additive) noise perturbations on image pixel as well as in graph structure. More broadly speaking, some concurrent works on arxiv also try to formulate and address the attack and robustness of combinatorial solvers (both neural and learning-free ones) [4,5]. Yet these existing attack/defense works for graph or specifically combinatorial optimization on graphs are all using heuristic and cannot provide a theoretically guaranteed robustness. 
* Instead our approach can certify (Eq. 6 and 9) a GM solver's robustness radius within which the perturbation will not change the solution, regardless of its attack strategy which can be even unknown. Our certification can be applied to both learning-based and -free solvers. 
* Our certified algorithms are more suitable for applications with high security requirements to ensure consistent prediction results with minimal loss of accuracy. We hope our research can shed light on the mission-critical applications. For example, the use of cross-modal graph matching can assist in the decision and analysis of autonomous driving. Combining with our certified robustness method can improve the safety of driving in reality. 
* In addition, our approach is promising to be extended to other combinatorial optimization solvers soon, forming a general framework that always guarantees robustness. We have updated Introduction section in the paper.

>***Q2: Information provided on experiments makes it hard to quantify the improvement. Need metrics like AUC to quantize the performance better. (is AUC even the right metric?)  It's very hard to quantify with the provided results (basically guessing about one line vs another)***
>
**R2:** Thank you for your valuable suggestion. 
To evaluate our method, we mainly follow evaluation criteria in [2] and use a plot to visualize the relationship between the robustness radius and the certified accuracy as in Fig.2. Although Fig. 2 allows us to visually compare the methods, a quantitative evaluation method is also needed.

Therefore, we totally agree with you that we need a metric to show the superiours of our method on the certified robustness over the whole dataset. Thus, we introduce Average Certified Radius (ACR) proposed by [3] to our methods as follows:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{x, y}\left[R\mathbb{1}(g(x)=y)\right].
$$
In our method, $g$ represents the smoothed function defined in Eq.4, $x$ represents the input node in the test dataset, and $y$ represents its ground truth matching node. $R$ represents the certified radius calculated by Eq.9, Eq.12, and Eq.13; meanwhile, $\mathbb{1}$ is an indicator function.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of the probabilistic robustness of graph-matching (GM) algorithms against norm-based adversarial perturbations. The authors develop new algorithms for randomized smoothing for GM by exploiting the structure of the problem. They start by decomposing the robust matching problem defined over the whole graph into subproblems defined over the individual nodes. Next, the noise for building the smoothed classifier is sampled from a joint gaussian distribution which is set up in a way to capture correlations between the different nodes in the graph. Experimental evaluation is performed on the popular Pascal-VOC dataset showing the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The technical contributions for building a probabilistically robust classifier for GM presented here are novel and solid. I wonder if structured distributions can also be used for improving the certified radius of vision classifiers.

2. The experimental results show that the proposed method can certify larger radii than standard baselines.

Weaknesses:
1. The problem and the approach are not well-motivated. While the robustness of vision models is necessary when deployed in safety-critical scenarios such as self-driving cars, it is not clear what security implications the non-robustness of graph matching can cause. The authors do not motivate the need for solving their problem but instead choose to start describing their approach in the introduction. 

2. Randomized smoothing makes inference slow due to the need for sample multiple points and also makes its prediction non-deterministic. Why is this a good approach for proving certified robustness for the GM setting?

3. The authors do not describe the impact of certified robustness on the accuracy of the classifier. Is there a tradeoff here?  For vision models, humans are the oracle and the goal is to achieve the same level of robustness as them. I do not see such an oracle for GM as even non-learned models are not robust. What level of accuracy and robustness is good in this setting?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and quality: Besides the issues with clarity mentioned above, I have the following comments for the authors:

1. Randomized smoothing for neural networks was introduced by https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03471 and not Cohen et al. The authors do not cite this. 

2.$\sum$ is an important hyperparameter controlling the robustness/accuracy tradeoff but the authors do not elaborate on the principles behind its construction (e.g., what properties it should satisfy). Eq. (10) seems a bit random to me, why would any other equation not work? The authors should consider performing a study on the impact of different choices for constructing $\sum$ on the certified robustness. 

3. In the equation for calculating $p_B$, the authors use $s_i \neq p_A$ which is semantically not correct. 

4. In figure 2, how are the y-axis values computed? are they averaged over the whole dataset? 

5. Would the radii be larger if one considered the robustness of three nodes at a time instead of a single node as considered here? In general, considering the robustness of the full matrix should reveal more correlations right? which should yield larger radii. Did you choose single-node decompositions because it makes the problem tractable?

6. The authors do not discuss the impact of sampling on the inference speed.

content.comment:
We appreciate the prompt reply and helpful suggestions. We have further clarified the motivations of random smoothing as follows. We sincerely hope you are satisfied with our response, and could provide us further instructions if necessary. 

We agree that the randomized smoothing [9] method may not provide 100% correct certification guarantee for strictly mission-critical tasks (e.g. space exploration). However, we would like to elaborate on our understanding of the robustness on some near-mission critical scenarios in one's daily life. 
* First, as described in works [19-23], deep learning has achieved tremendous success over the years, and it starts to be deployed in various real-world scenes, including some near-mission critical applications (e.g. autonomous driving, face recognition in ATMs). Meanwhile, deep learning approaches have been shown inevitably vulnerable to adversarial attacks [20-23]. As a result, the study of robustness against adversarial attacks has drawn intensive attention in recent years. Currently, typical robustness-based methods include adversarial training [24,25], regularization techniques, certified defenses [9,13,14,28-30], etc. Although these methods have their own strengths and weaknesses, they are all promising researches to promote the more reliable deployment of deep learning models in real-world near-mission critical applications [19]. 
* Second, we would like to clarify that, in near-mission critical applications, 100% correct guarantee is not a must though ideally preferable. Actually, a robustness method is also desirable in practice, as long as it can provide a provable guarantee to control the uncertainty within a certain high confidence interval. For example, as shown in industry standard of autonomous driving [26,27], it usually involves a comprehensive safety assessment indicator which indeed permits different confidence levels of safety assurances. In such near-mission critical scenes, we believe a randomized smoothing method can well satisfy the robustness requirement with probabilistic and controllable guarantees. Therefore, we modify our description "mission-critical" to "near-mission critical". 
* Third, we would like to highlight again that compared with other defense methods, certified defenses can further guarantee the robustness of the network under any type of attacks (even unknown ones). Bound propagation [13,14] and randomized smoothing [9] are both representative methods of certified defenses. Bound propagation is a deterministic certified defense method, yet unfortunately, it has difficulties in scaling to large models. Recently, randomized smoothing has emerged as a certification approach from the probabilistic paradigm that scales well to large models and datasets. Since the model for graph matching is relatively large, only the randomized smoothing can be used to certify its robustness at present. Moreover, there are two other distinct advantages of applying randomized smoothing to graph matching. One is that randomized smoothing [9] treats all functions (regardless of deep learning or non-learning based graph matching functions) as black-box models, thus it has the potential for direct extension to other combinatorial optimization problems. The other is that graph structure as a whole conveys important information, so we use a smoothing distribution $\Sigma$ to construct correlations between nodes.

To sum up, we discuss the robustness of near-mission critical scenarios as well as the strengths and weaknesses of randomized smoothing [9] and bound propagation [13,14] certification methods. (We believe they are orthogonal and supplementary to each other.) However, detailed comparison and justification for these two categories of works are actually beyond the scope of our rebuttal, and they are not the topics of our paper.

> 
**R1:** 
* **Randomized smoothing (Cohen et al.2019) [9] is probabilistic yet can be of arbitrary small uncertainty.** We agree that randomized smoothing is a probabilistic approach. In our method, the exact values of $p_{A}$ and $p_{B}$ in Section 4.2 cannot be obtained, and so we follow the Monte Carlo sampling method mentioned in [9] to get the lower bound of $p_{A}$ and upper bound of $p_{B}$. To evaluate the reliability of sampling, we also use hypothesis test [18] as in [9] by using $\alpha$ to represent the probability of getting incorrect matching results. This is the standard and general results under randomized smoothing. In this paper, we set $\alpha=0.001$, and so there is a high probability (99.9% in this paper) to ensure the certification. $\alpha$ can be set arbitrarily small hence in theory our method is highly reliable and can be applied to mission-critical applications. 
* **There are two important properties of randomized smoothing [9] that make it suitable for the robustness certification of graph matching.** **First**, randomized smoothing [9] treats the model as a black box, so it can be easily extended to more graph matching functions. **Second**, it is usable for large-scale models, which is also necessary for graph matching functions which need to process image inputs. content.comment:
>***Q5: $\Sigma$ is an important hyperparameter controlling the robustness/accuracy tradeoff but the authors do not elaborate on the principles behind its construction (e.g., what properties it should satisfy).  The authors should consider performing a study on the impact of different choices for constructing $\Sigma$ on the certified robustness.***
>
**R5:** Thank you for your valuable questions. $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ should be a positive definite matrix in the paper which enables us to derive certified space using linear transformations in Appendix. Therefore, we construct $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ by constructing $\mathbf{B}$ using $\mathbf{B}^{\top} \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{\Sigma}$, thus we can maintain the properties of $\mathbf{\Sigma}$.

In our work, we use Eq.10 to construct $\mathbf{B}$ where $d_{mn}$ is an euclidean distance in our work, which is a method to reveal the correlation between nodes. And we evaluate the effect of the correlations strength in $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ on robustness in Fig.4(a). We compare the experimental results of retaining correlations, partially retaining correlations (for example, 20% means that the correlation coefficients of the top 20% are retained), and completely removing correlations to demonstrate the effectiveness of the $\mathbf{\Sigma}$. The correlation enhancement in $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ improves the robust performance overall.

Moreover, we fully agree with your proposal to performing a study on the impact of different choices for constructing $\mathbf{\Sigma}$. Therefore, we use cosine similarity, pearson similarity, dice similarity to construct $\mathbf{B}$ respectively and then verify the effect of the different $\Sigma$ obtained on the robustness results. We introduce the similarity as follows:
For two points in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$: $A=\left(a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n\right)$ and $B=\left(b_1, b_2, \cdots, b_n\right)$, where $A$ and $B$ cannot be zero point at the same time:
* $\operatorname{Cosine} \operatorname{Similarity}(A, B)=\frac{A \cdot B}{\|A\|\_2 \cdot\|B\|\_2}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2}} \in[-1,1].$
* $\operatorname{Pearson} \operatorname{Similarity}(A, B)=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(A, B)}{\sigma_A \cdot \sigma_B}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}\left(a_i-\bar{A}\right) \cdot\left(b_i-\bar{B}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n\left(a_i-\bar{A}\right)^2} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n\left(b_i-\bar{B}\right)^2}} \in [-1,1],$
where $\bar{A}=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i / n, \bar{B}=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i / n$.
* $\operatorname{Dice} \operatorname{Similarity}(A, B)=\frac{2 \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n\left(a_i^2+b_i^2\right)} \in [-1,1]$.

We compare the certified robustness using four methods to construct matrix $\mathbf{B}$ on NGMv2 GM algorithm and on Pascal VOC dataset.

We calculate the ACR $\|\|\delta\|\|_{\text{lower}}$ of four different RS-type methods ($\sigma$ = 5) and four GM methods.

| RS     | 4.189     | 2.880     | 2.745     | 2.037     |

>***Q4: Randomized smoothing for neural networks was introduced by https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03471 and not Cohen et al. The authors do not cite this.***
>
**R4:** Thank you for your suggestion and we agree with your comment. (Lecuyer et al.2019) [8] proposed randomized smoothing firstly as a certified adversarial defense, and used it to train the first certifiably robust classifier for ImageNet. However, its guarantees are loose, (Cohen et al, 2019) [9] solved this problem and proposed the tight robustness guarantee for randomized smoothing. content.title: Response to Reviewer 7S16 (1/4)
content.comment:
>***Q1: The authors do not motivate the need for solving their problem but instead choose to start describing their approach in the introduction.***
>
**R1:** 
Thank you very much for your valuable suggestion.  We plan to add more related to motivations in the introduction.  In detail, our motivations are as follows:
As one of the common combinatorial optimization problems and most important research topics in the graph domain with wide applications in computer vision and pattern recognition, graph matching has been intensively studied over the decades, such as image keypoint matching [1], scene graph discovery [2] and vision-text retrieval [3].
* Studies on robustness of machine learning models have attracted wide attention, while the robustness of combinatorial solvers (graph matching is one the cases) is an emerging and unmatured topic whose importance has also been elaborated in the previous works [4]. 
* Graph matching (GM) problem is an intensively studied combinatorial optimization problem in computer vision and pattern recognition (see the surveys [15,16,17]). CVPR'22 paper [4] raised people's attention that neural GM solvers can be sensitive to (additive) noise perturbations on image pixel as well as in graph structure. More broadly speaking, some concurrent works on arxiv also try to formulate and address the attack and robustness of combinatorial solvers (both neural and learning-free ones) [5,6]. Yet these existing attack/defense works for graph or specifically combinatorial optimization on graphs are all using heuristic and cannot provide a theoretically guaranteed robustness. 
* Instead our approach can certify (Eq. 6 and 9) a GM solver's robustness radius within which the perturbation will not change the solution, regardless of its attack strategy which can be even unknown. Our certification can be applied to both learning-based and -free solvers. 
* Our certified algorithms are more suitable for applications with high security requirements to ensure consistent prediction results with minimal loss of accuracy. We hope our research can shed light on the mission-critical applications. For example, the use of cross-modal graph matching can assist in the decision and analysis of autonomous driving. Combining with our certified robustness method can improve the safety of driving in reality. 
* In addition, our approach is promising to be extended to other combinatorial optimization solvers soon, forming a general framework that always guarantees robustness. We have updated Introduction section in the paper.

>***Q2: Randomized smoothing makes inference slow due to the need for sample multiple points and also makes its prediction non-deterministic. Why is this a good approach for proving certified robustness for the GM setting?***
>
**R2:** Thank you for your valuable questions and we fully agree with you about the drawbacks of randomized smoothing. The main reasons why introducing the randomized smoothing approach to address the certified robustness of GM are as follows:
* First, randomized smoothing is feasible on large networks, therefore it is suitable for deep graph matching networks. Moreover, it makes no assumption about the base function’s architecture, thus a general certified robustness framework for many types of graph matching functions can be constructed, which also facilitates subsequent extensions to more combinatorial optimization problems.
Other common methods to certify robustness include: Lipschitz constant method [11,12], Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) methods [13,14], etc. These two methods are relatively flexible and don not require inference by sampling, but they have requirements on the network structure and the robust boundary obtained by the calculation is relatively loose. More importantly, they are not suitable for use in deep GM algorithms and Pascal VOC dataset.
* Second, we find that the smoothing distribution in randomized smoothing can be used to represent the structural correlation in the graph matching input which is beneficial to improve the overall certified robustness.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,
We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments and have updated our paper accordingly. In our general response, we give quick response for two important aspects: i) significance and ii) our added new treatment on certifying the solution $X$ with structure (we currently put it in appendix while we can also move it to main paper upon request).

**1) Significance and impact (reviewer BhnR, 7S16):**
Foremost, we try to address and clarify some common concerns. In the paper, we propose a general framework for incorporating existing RS-based techniques for certifying graph matching solvers by converting the relaxed matching $\mathbf{S}$ (by an arbitrary relaxed GM solver) to node matching. We believe robustness certification for the GM solver is a good starting point for the more open problem w.r.t. certification for combinatorial solvers (see our detailed response in below for each reviewer).


**2) Certification on the structure of $X$  (reviewer n9K9, 7S16):**
We also feel inspirational by the valuable comments of Reviewer n9K9 (Q4) and 7S16 (Q8) to better certify the overall robustness of solution matrix $X$, and we did have already developed further technology in this regard and put the content in the Appendix E. (We are also happy to put it in the main text and update the main pdf upon your feedback).

- Definition of smoothed function for $X$
We define a certified robustness to the overall $X$, which means that when the perturbation to the input is within a certain range, the output $X$ matrix is guaranteed to remain constant with a confidence $c$. Consider a graph matching problem from input space to partial permutation matrices $\mathcal{X}$. As discussed above, randomized smoothing (RS) is a technique for constructing a smoothed function $g$ from an arbitrary base function $f$. When queried at the input $\left(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1}, \mathbf{z}^{2}\right)$, the smoothed function $g$ returns whichever matrix $X$ the base function $f$ is most likely to return when $\mathbf{z}^{1}$ is perturbed by noise:
$$
g=\underset{X \in \mathcal{X}}{\arg \max } \mathbb{P}(f\left(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1}+\varepsilon, \mathbf{z}^{2}\right)=X),\\
\text{where} \  \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}\right).
$$
The distribution of additive noise $\varepsilon$ is a joint Gaussian distribution matrix whose variance $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ represents the correlations between nodes. In addition, $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ is a hyperparameter for certified function which controls the robustness/accuracy trade-off.
- Robustness Guarantee for $X$
We define a robustness guarantee with confidence $c \in [0,1]$, which ensures that the similarity between the output matrix calculated by $g$ and its ground truth matrix $X_{g}$ is not less than $c$. Suppose that when the base function $f$ solves $\left(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1}+\varepsilon, \mathbf{z}^{2}\right)$, its output matrices whose similarity to $X_{g}$ is not less than $c$ are returned with probability $p$:
$$
\mathcal{X^{0}} = \{X_{i} \vert \frac{X_{i} \cdot X_{g} }{X_{g} \cdot X_{g}} \geq c, X_{i} \in \mathcal{X}\},\\
p = \mathbb{P}(X_{i} \vert X_{i} \in \mathcal{X^{0}})
$$
Our main result is that smoothed function $g$ is robust within a $\ell_{2}$ certified space, which also holds if we replace $p$ with a lower bound $\underline{p}$.

**Theorem** *Let $f$ be a matching function, $g$ be defined as in the equation above, and $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}\right)$. Suppose $X_{A} \in \mathcal{X^{0}}$ and $\underline{p}\in (\frac{1}{2},1]$ satisfy:
$$
% \mathbb{P}(X_{A} \vert X_{A} \in \mathcal{X^{0}}) \geq \underline{p}.
\mathbb{P}(f\left(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1}+\varepsilon, \mathbf{z}^{2}\right)=X_{A}, X_{A} \in \mathcal{X^{0}})\geq \underline{p}.
$$
Then we can get the certified $\ell_{2}$ space for the addictive noise $\delta$:
$$
\|\|\delta^{\top} \mathbf{B}^{-1} \|\|< \Phi^{-1}\left(\underline{p}\right),
$$
which guarantees $g\left(\mathcal{G}\_{1},\mathcal{G}\_{2},\mathbf{z}^{1}+\delta, \mathbf{z}^{2}\right) \in \mathcal{X^{0}}$.  $\mathbf{B}^{\top} \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{\Sigma}$ and $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{1} \times n_{1}}$ is a full rank and real symmetric matrix based on the node correlation in node matrix $\mathbf{z}^{1}$.*
Through this theorem we can get the certified robustness of $X$ as a whole. For specific details and related experimental results, please refer to Appendix E in the paper.

content.comment:
Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,

We would like to express our sincere thanks to the four reviewers for their time and valuable suggestions. In the rebuttal, we have elaborated our explanations, included more experiments, and revised our paper following all reviewers’ suggestions.

Based on reviewers' prompt feedbacks, we are encouraged that the concerns of reviewers BhnR, n9K9, Sgyn have been mostly addressed, and reviewer BhnR improved the score (from 5 to 6).

We hope and think reviewer 7S16 also acknowledged our response, except for a debatable dispute (which we really appreciate) on the motivation of this paper. Meanwhile, we note that reviewers BhnR and Sgyn showed satisfaction to our further explanation of our motivation, in our response.

Below we try to summarize the rebuttal and hope it could facilitate your final evaluation.

* We explain and supplement the motivation of this work (Reviewer BhnR, 7S16), including the significance and impact of the robustness certification for the GM solver, which is acknowledged by the reviewers.
* We explain why we implement the robustness certification for GM solver based on the randomized smoothing framework (Reviewer Sgyn, 7S16). **First**, we explain the significant differences between this work and the previous randomized smoothing framework (Reviewer Sgyn), and we get a positive reply from the reviewer Sgyn. **Second**, we compare the pros/cons of the randomized smoothing framework and other methods for certifiable robustness, arguing that the randomized smoothing framework is suitable for certifying the robustness for GM solvers and it has the potential for direct extension to other combinatorial optimization problems (Reviewer 7S16) -- e.g. for node labeling based solvers: ["Learning Combinatorial Node Labeling Algorithms"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03594). **Third**, as for **the concern by reviewer 7S16** whether randomized smoothing (RS) is suitable for mission-critical applications, we also give a detailed response. Reviewer 7S16 thought that RS is a probabilistic framework and cannot ensure zero mistake and therefore may not be suitable for mission-critical applications. We have to say we do not fully agree and this dispute may go beyond the technical part of this paper: it is more about the applicability of RS itself which has been well acknowledged and used in the community. In fact, we are in the optimistic side and RS is exactly a mathematical tool to endow a machine learning module a degree (lower bound) of certification (up to infinitely close to 100% correctness by setting a small enough $\alpha$). We also fully respect reviewer's 7S16's rigorousness and modify the wording "mission-critical" to "near-mission critical". Moreover, we believe there are still broad areas using our technique, especially with the human-specified $\alpha$ to achieve almost controllable guarantees.
* We also feel inspirational by the comments of Reviewer n9K9 and 7S16 on better certifying the overall robustness of solution matrix $X$. We supplement with further techniques (including definitions and experiments) to make the paper more comprehensive and pertinent.
* In terms of experimental evaluation, **first** we adopt reviewer BhnR's suggestion and introduce Average Certified Radius (ACR) to quantize the performance. **Second**, we add relationship tables of accuracy (accuracy of base solvers, standard accuracy and certified accuracy of certified solvers) and radius to show the impact of certified robustness on the matching accuracy of the solvers based on the suggestion of reviewer 7S16. **Third**, we perform a study on the impact of different choices for constructing $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ on the certified robustness based on the suggestion of reviewer 7S16. The above experiments are a good supplement to our work, and the experimental results have also been recognized by the reviewers (BhnR and 7S16). **Fourth**, we also explain the experimental protocol in more detail (Reviwer BhnR), and have made modifications to the presentation of the paper (Reviewer 7S16, Sgyn, n9K9).

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
A well-known NP-hard problem is graph matching, GM (as opposed to the polynomial-time solvable matching problem in a single graph): matching between two---or more---given graphs in order to maximize an affinity score of the matching. This work considers the (probabilistic) robustness of algorithms for GM algorithms against norm-bounded adversarial perturbations; it develops new algorithms for randomized “smoothing”. The robust matching problem on the graph is decomposed into subproblems defined over the nodes; the noise for building the smoothed classifier is sampled from a joint Gaussian that is defined to capture correlations between the different nodes. Experimental evaluation is performed on a popular dataset and is generally promising (e.g., can certify larger radii than could earlier approaches). The paper is solid overall.

The setup needs to be motivated better: while robustness is critical in some applications (e.g., vision in self-driving cars), the security implications of non-robust GM needs to be described in more depth. Furthermore, randomized smoothing makes inference slow, and needs to be motivated better for  certified GM robustness. Even the work of references [13,14] in the paper is applicable as far as the theory goes (although scalability is an issue): there appears to be no bottleneck in GM that will stymie [13,14] from inferring correlations between nodes. Also, a stronger case can be made that a smoothed classifier can solve security problems when safety is critical.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The utility of robustness for the studied graph-matching problem needs to be made clearer (as compared to obvious settings such as vision in self-driving vehicles); the fact that inference gets slowed down also has to be addressed.
